One-of-6 Mopar: A Closer Look at the World's Most Expensive 1970 Road Runner Convertible
9 photos
Photo: CARFINDER/YouTube
About a week ago, I showed you a super-rare 1970 Plymouth Road Runner convertible that crossed the block for over $200,000 . Well, if you're a fan of factory pink Mopars, I have a full video walkaround of the car to show you.
The vehicle was shot while sitting on display before it went under the hammer in late October 2026. The Road Runner was auctioned off at Mecum's Dallas/Fort Worth 2026 auction, changing hands for $269,500. The sum included a 10% buyer's premium.
The sticker makes this Road Runner the third most expensive 1970 iteration ever sold at public auction. It's also the most expensive convertible of its kind, as well as the priciest 1970 Road Runner with a standard engine, regardless of the body style.
While the selling price is a bit surprising for a Mopar fitted with a 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter) V8, it's not exactly shocking given the color. These factory pink Mopars have become increasingly more expensive in recent years, mainly because they're super rare .
Called Moulin Rouge on Plymouth cars and Panther Pink on Dodge models, FM3 is one of the 10 high-impact colors that Chrysler offered between 1969 and 1973. This hue is rare for quite a few reasons. For starters, pink was only available as a Spring Color in 1970. The option was on offer for only a couple of months.
Second, it was far from popular. Considered too feminine for a muscle car, it was ordered on only a tiny fraction of Mopars sold in 1970. Third, many of these vehicles were repainted in different colors by their second owners. Most people simply hated pink muscle cars back in the day.
This car is also rare due to the convertible top. Plymouth introduced a Road Runner drop top in 1969, selling just 1,890 units. Despite this low figure, the division kept the convertible in showrooms in 1970. Sales dropped even lower, with only 658 examples rolling off the assembly line.
Of these, three were ordered with the mighty 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi, while 34 were fitted with the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) Six-Barrel V8. The remaining 621 units were delivered with the standard 383-cubic-inch powerplant. This Road Runner is also an automatic car, which makes it one of 429 built with this drivetrain combo.
How many of them were FM3 pink? Well, specific numbers are not available, but Mopar experts estimate that only 44 Road Runners were ordered in this hue in 1970. Only six of them were convertibles, and it's believed that just three are still around. Moreover, this example is said to be the only one with a matching-numbers drivetrain.
So, how come it's the most expensive 1970 convertible given that we have three more desirable Hemi units on the loose? Well, those have yet to go under the hammer at public events. They would probably fetch much more, but for that to happen, the owners would have to be willing to part ways with them. And it's unclear if all three are still around.
And interestingly enough, this pink Mopar fetched more than the priciest 1970 Road Runner with the rarer Six-Barrel V8. The previous record was set in 2025, when an unrestored V-code drop top changed hands at public auction for an impressive $220,000.
But that's enough history for today. Now hit the play button below for a full walkaround of this bright pink ragtop.
